title: Java Syntax and Program Structure
description: The anatomy of a Java program: classes, the main method, statements, blocks, comments, and naming conventions.
objectives: Understand the required structure of a runnable Java program
Understand the main() method's exact signature
Use comments and follow Java naming conventions

content.heading: Classes and the main Method
content.body:
Every piece of Java code lives inside a class (there is no code at the top level of a file, unlike Python or C's global scope). A runnable Java application needs exactly one method with the signature public static void main(String[] args) — this is the entry point the JVM looks for. public means it's callable from outside the class; static means it belongs to the class itself, not to any particular instance (so the JVM can call it without first creating an object); void means it returns nothing; String[] args holds any command-line arguments passed to the program.

Statements in Java each end with a semicolon; related statements are grouped into blocks delimited by curly braces {}, which define the body of a class, method, loop, or conditional — this is a key structural difference from Python, which uses indentation instead.

content.heading: Comments and Naming Conventions
content.body:
Java supports single-line comments (// comment), multi-line comments (/* comment */), and documentation comments (/** ... */, used by the Javadoc tool to auto-generate API documentation from specially-formatted tags like @param and @return).

Java naming conventions: classes use PascalCase (BankAccount), methods and variables use camelCase (calculateTotal, accountBalance), and constants use UPPER_SNAKE_CASE (MAX_SIZE). Identifiers must start with a letter, $, or _, followed by letters, digits, $, or _, and cannot be one of Java's reserved keywords (class, public, static, void, if, for, and so on).

content.explanation: Everything is nested inside the Greeter class; main() is the entry point the JVM calls first. The Javadoc comment above the class demonstrates documentation-style commenting.

keyPoints: All Java code lives inside a class — there's no true top-level/global code
public static void main(String[] args) is the required, exact entry-point signature
Braces {} delimit blocks; semicolons ; terminate statements
PascalCase for classes, camelCase for methods/variables, UPPER_SNAKE_CASE for constants
commonMistakes: Misspelling or mistyping the main method signature so the JVM can't find an entry point
Forgetting a semicolon at the end of a statement
Naming a class file differently from its public class name (Java requires them to match)
